opus-5.5.text:
Well, if I had to pick one, it's that transformers don't really reason. They interpolate, extraordinarily well, over a vast amount of data, and that gets you surprisingly far. But when you push them to compose knowledge in genuinely new ways, chaining many steps where each one has to be exactly right, they become brittle. You get these confident hallucinations, and you can't fix that by just scaling up, because the architecture has no built-in notion of a rule being true or false. It only has a notion of a continuation being likely.

Closely related is data inefficiency. A child learns what a dog is from a handful of examples. A transformer needs to see the whole internet, and even then it hasn't learned the concept in a robust, reusable way. That tells you something important is missing in the inductive bias.

My view has always been that each of the major schools of machine learning has a piece of the puzzle. The connectionists have learning from raw data and gradient descent. The symbolists have composition, logic, and the ability to generalize from very little. The Bayesians have uncertainty. Transformers are the triumph of one tribe, but the master algorithm, if we get there, has to unify them. So what I most want is an architecture where learning and reasoning are the same operation, not a neural net with a symbolic system bolted on as a tool. Something you can trust when it says "this follows from that," and that can learn a rule once and apply it everywhere.

I think we're closer to that than people realize, but it's not going to come from making the context window longer.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the one I'd put at the top is that transformers don't really reason. They do something that looks like reasoning, because they've absorbed enormous amounts of text that contains reasoning, and they can pattern-match their way to the next step surprisingly often. But there's no mechanism in there that guarantees the conclusion follows from the premises. It's all association. And the attention mechanism, when you strip away the hype, is essentially a soft, differentiable form of nearest-neighbor retrieval. It's a kernel machine. That's very powerful for interpolating within the data you've seen, and it's very bad at extrapolating beyond it.

So what I'd most like to overcome is this: I want models that can learn things like compositional structure, that can take a rule they've learned in one place and apply it systematically somewhere they've never seen, and that can do it with a small amount of data instead of the entire internet. Humans do this constantly. A child learns what a verb is from a handful of examples and then generalizes to every verb they ever encounter. Transformers need to see millions of instances, and even then they're brittle at the edges.

And I'd argue the reason is that we threw out the symbolic baby with the bathwater. For decades we had logic, we had structured representations, we had the ability to say "this implies that" and have it actually mean something. Then deep learning came along, it worked, and the field decided all of that was obsolete. I think it's not. I think the real breakthrough is going to be a unified learner that combines the statistical strength of neural nets with the compositional strength of symbolic methods. That's what I was getting at with the master algorithm. Markov logic was one attempt at it; there will be better ones.

The other thing I'd mention, which is related, is that transformers can't learn continuously. You train them, you freeze them, and then they live in that frozen state until somebody spends another hundred million dollars retraining them. That's absurd. An intelligent system should be learning every second it's running, incorporating new evidence, revising what it believes. The fact that we've built the most expensive machines in history and they can't update a belief without a full retraining run is, to me, a sign that we're missing something fundamental, not just an engineering detail.

astra-6.text:
The limitation I’d most like us to overcome is their ability to generalize beyond the kinds of examples they’ve seen. Transformers are extraordinarily good at learning patterns, but that’s not the same as discovering a rule and reliably applying it in a new situation. They can do that in some cases, but it’s still brittle.

This is where I think combining learning with symbolic reasoning becomes interesting. You want a system that learns from messy data, but can also represent variables, relations, and rules, and compose those into longer chains of reasoning. The challenge is to learn those abstractions rather than have a programmer supply them all. More scale may help, but we shouldn’t assume scale alone will solve the problem.

sol-6.1.text: The limitation I’d most like to overcome is their inability to reliably reason beyond the patterns they’ve seen in training. Transformers are extraordinarily good at learning those patterns, but we still struggle to get systematic generalization: learning a rule and then applying it correctly in a genuinely new situation. I think the challenge is to combine that ability to learn from data with explicit reasoning, while retaining uncertainty. You want a system that can learn, compose what it learns, and recognize when it doesn’t know.
